meta.location: The land of Nephi, mount Antipas, the city of Nephi
principles: Dissenters who become worse than the people they join

world_behind.title: The Lamanite army did not want to fight
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says they feared the king and feared the war, and the greater part refused the proclamation. Amalickiah's opportunity comes from that refusal.

world_behind.title: The king hands him the loyal troops
world_behind.text: Verse 3 has the king, angry at the disobedience, give Amalickiah command of the obedient part and order him to compel the rest. The instrument is supplied by the target.

world_behind.title: Mormon states the plan before it runs
world_behind.text: Verses 4 and 8 both give the intention: dethrone the king and take the kingdom. The reader watches each step knowing where it goes.

world_behind.title: Lehonti refuses three times
world_behind.text: Verses 11 and 12 have him decline to come down, and Amalickiah climbs most of the way up on the fourth ask. The caution is real and it is not enough.

world_behind.title: The Lamanite succession rule is given
world_behind.text: Verse 17 says the second leader becomes chief if the chief is killed. Mormon supplies the custom in the verse before the poisoning.

world_behind.title: The murder uses a Nephite custom
world_behind.text: Verse 23 says raising a bowing man was a token of peace the Lamanites had taken from the Nephites. The gesture is what puts the king in reach.

world_behind.title: The witnesses are the killers
world_behind.text: Verse 34 has Amalickiah bring the servant who did it, and the men with him, to testify that the king's own servants did it. Mormon says the queen was satisfied.

words.text: Treated at Alma 12:4, where Alma tells Zeezrom his plan was subtle. The record uses the word twice and the King James Bible never. Mormon applies it to Amalickiah in the same verse that gives his aim.

Treated at Mosiah 29:21, where king Mosiah argues that an unrighteous king can be removed only with much contention. Amalickiah does it in thirty verses, and the record uses the word twice more in this chapter.

A message sent by an envoy. It appears three times in the record, and never in the King James Bible, twice in this chapter. The first carries a secret offer to Lehonti; the second carries a lie to the queen.

Stages, small increments. Treated at Mosiah 21:16. Two uses of the phrase "by degrees" here, and none in the King James Bible. Mormon uses it of the poison given to Lehonti, which describes a killing designed to look like an illness.

Clotted blood. The word occurs once in this record and once in the King James Bible, in a law about an ox that gores. Mormon uses the noun of the king lying in it while Amalickiah pretends to be angry.

Habitual laziness. The word occurs once in scripture. Mormon lists it with lasciviousness in his account of what the dissenters became, and the whole verse is his explanation of why they turned out worse.

phrases.term: They feared to displease the king, and they also feared to go to battle
phrases.text: Two fears pulling opposite ways, and the second wins. Mormon gives the Lamanite army's refusal as a calculation rather than as rebellion, and that refusal is the opening Amalickiah uses.

phrases.term: He being a very subtle man to do evil therefore he laid the plan in his heart
phrases.text: Mormon names the method and the aim together. The plan exists before the campaign, and every move in the next thirty verses is reported against it.

phrases.term: It was not Amalickiah's intention to give them battle
phrases.text: The order he was given and the thing he means to do are different. Mormon states the divergence plainly, so the reader watches an obedient-looking march with the real purpose in view.

phrases.term: He sent again the fourth time his message unto Lehonti, desiring that he would come down
phrases.text: Persistence past three refusals. Amalickiah climbs nearly to the camp and adds a concession: bring your guards. The safeguard is what makes the meeting acceptable.

phrases.term: If he would make him a second leader over the whole army
phrases.text: The price Amalickiah asks looks modest. He offers to betray his own men and requests the second place, and verse 17 explains what second place is worth.

phrases.term: It was the custom among the Lamanites, if their chief leader was killed, to appoint the second leader
phrases.text: Mormon supplies the rule immediately before the poisoning. The placement makes the reader see the bargain of verse 13 for what it was.

phrases.term: Administer poison by degrees to Lehonti, that he died
phrases.text: The killing given in half a verse. The method leaves no moment of violence and no visible cause, and the succession does the rest.

phrases.term: As a token of peace, which custom they had taken from the Nephites
phrases.text: Mormon traces the gesture to its origin. A Nephite habit of peace, adopted by Lamanites, is the thing that lets a Nephite dissenter reach the king's heart.

phrases.term: Behold, the servants of the king have stabbed him to the heart
phrases.text: The lie is raised as a cry by the men who did it, seconds after the act. Verse 27 has Amalickiah pretending to be angry and ordering a pursuit of the innocent.

phrases.term: Thus Amalickiah, by his fraud, gained the hearts of the people
phrases.text: Mormon's summary of the whole sequence. He names it fraud twice, here and in verse 35, and does not credit any of it to ability.
Mormon interrupts his own sentence to say he finds it hard to explain. The dissenters had the same instruction and knowledge, and became more hardened and ferocious than the people they joined.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: The record counts the embassies
verses.text: A negotiation that could have been summarised in a clause is instead numbered. The message goes out at night, Lehonti "durst not go down"; Amalickiah "sent again the second time," and again "the third time," and then, having climbed most of the way up the mountain himself, "he sent again the fourth time." Four refusals and four sendings are tracked in three verses. The detail that makes the fourth work is spatial, not rhetorical: the man asking has moved so close that coming down means walking a few yards.

verses.label: v. 10–19
verses.title: A man who exists for ten verses
verses.text: Lehonti is named ten times, and every one of them falls between verses 10 and 19. He appears in no other chapter of scripture. Inside those ten verses he is invited four times, comes down, takes the enemy camp, is made chief, is poisoned "by degrees," and dies. The word mount behaves the same way, standing eight times and only in verses 7 through 12. A chapter that runs thirty-six verses gives this whole episode a vocabulary that begins and ends inside it.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: The rule supplied one verse before it is needed
verses.text: Verse 17 stops the story to state a custom: "if their chief leader was killed, to appoint the second leader to be their chief leader." Verse 18 kills the chief leader. Verse 19 appoints the second. The aside is not placed where the custom is first relevant, which would be verse 13, nor at the chapter's head as background. It sits in the one position where a reader who did not have it would not understand the next two verses, and it is the only explanatory aside in the first thirty verses.

verses.label: v. 22–24
verses.title: The gesture, and where it came from
verses.text: The murder turns on a courtesy, and the record traces the courtesy's origin. The servants bow, "and it came to pass that the king put forth his hand to raise them, as was the custom with the Lamanites, as a token of peace, which custom they had taken from the Nephites." A Lamanite king is killed while performing a peace gesture his people had borrowed from the Nephites, at the hands of a Nephite dissenter. The record does not draw the irony out; it states the borrowing in a subordinate clause and moves to the stabbing in the next verse.

verses.label: v. 25–26
verses.title: A lie the reader can check clause by clause
verses.text: The false report is given in full: "the servants of the king have stabbed him to the heart, and he has fallen and they have fled; behold, come and see." Set against verses 24 and 25, every clause is true except the first four words. He was stabbed to the heart, he did fall, and the servants of the king did flee, which verse 25 has already reported. The lie works by attaching a true account to the wrong subject, and the reader is in a position to test it only because the record narrated the killing first.

verses.label: v. 32–35
verses.title: Witnesses produced by the man they clear
verses.text: Queen is used six times in this chapter and only in verses 32 through 35. She does the one sensible thing in the chapter: she asks for testimony. "Amalickiah took the same servant that slew the king, and all them who were with him, and went in unto the queen... and they all testified unto her that the king was slain by his own servants." The witnesses to the murder are the murderers, produced by the man who ordered it. Verse 35 gives the outcome in the record's own terms, "thus by his fraud, and by the assistance of his cunning servants, he obtained the kingdom."

verses.label: v. 36
verses.title: The abridger says he does not understand it
verses.text: The chapter closes with an aside the record makes nowhere else: "it is strange to relate." The phrase occurs once in the volume, here. What puzzles the writer is not the murders but the dissenters, who had "the same instruction and the same information of the Nephites" and yet became "more wild, wicked and ferocious than the Lamanites." Thirty-five verses of poisoning, assassination and forged testimony pass without editorial comment; the thing that draws one is a change of character in men who knew better.

chapter.title: Every move is made with somebody else's hand
chapter.text: The king's own troops, Lehonti's ambition, a servant's poison, another servant's knife, the queen's request for witnesses. Amalickiah is never the one holding the weapon.

chapter.title: Mormon tells the reader the plan first
chapter.text: Verses 4 and 8 give the aim before the sequence runs. The chapter is written so that nothing surprises, which puts the attention on method.

chapter.title: Lehonti's caution was correct and insufficient
chapter.text: Three refusals and an escort. What defeated him was an offer that made the meeting look like his own victory.

chapter.title: The succession rule is placed to be seen
chapter.text: Verse 17 sits between the bargain and the poison. Mormon could have given the custom anywhere and gives it at the moment it explains everything.

chapter.title: A peace custom becomes the murder weapon
chapter.text: Verse 23 explains the gesture and its origin before it is used against him: the king put forth his hand to raise them "as was the custom with the Lamanites, as a token of peace, which custom they had taken from the Nephites." Verse 24 then reports the stabbing in the same motion, "when he had raised the first from the ground, behold he stabbed the king to the heart." The record supplies the etiquette, its borrowed source, and its exploitation across two consecutive verses.

chapter.title: The false account is built to survive questioning
chapter.text: The false account is quoted at verse 26, "the servants of the king have stabbed him to the heart, and he has fallen and they have fled," and the evidence offered is the flight itself. Verse 27 has the killer manufacture the corroboration, "Whosoever loved the king, let him go forth, and pursue his servants," which produces the pursuit at verse 28 and the flight to Zarahemla at verse 29. When the queen demands witnesses at verse 34, the men who did the pursuing supply them.

chapter.title: Mormon calls it fraud, not skill
chapter.text: Twice, in verses 30 and 35. He describes a competent operation and refuses the vocabulary of competence.

chapter.title: The closing verse is the chapter's real subject
chapter.text: Verse 36 states the puzzle in three parallel clauses, "having the same instruction and the same information of the Nephites, yea, having been instructed in the same knowledge of the Lord," and then the outcome, "more hardened and impenitent, and more wild, wicked and ferocious than the Lamanites." Between the premise and the conclusion the compiler inserts four words in his own voice, "it is strange to relate." He does not supply a cause, and the phrase appears nowhere else in these books.

applications.title: Watch who benefits when you are handed authority
applications.text: The king gave Amalickiah troops out of anger at somebody else. When something lands in your hands because a third party is annoyed, ask what it is actually for.

applications.title: Read the persistence as the message
applications.text: Amalickiah sent for Lehonti a second and a third time after the first refusal, and then climbed most of the mountain to send a fourth. When someone will not accept a no and keeps raising what they will spend to get a meeting, the size of the effort tells you the size of what they expect to gain by it.

applications.title: Be careful when the safeguard is your own idea
applications.text: Lehonti brought guards and still lost. When you agree to something risky because you have arranged a protection, check whether the protection addresses the actual danger.

applications.title: Distrust an offer that costs the other person nothing real
applications.text: Amalickiah asked only for second place. When someone requests something small and specific, work out what that position is worth to them.

applications.title: Read the succession rule before you take the second seat
applications.text: The chapter stops the action to explain that Lamanite custom moved the second leader into the first place when the chief was killed, which is what made the poisoning worth doing. Before you accept a deputy role, or hand one out, find out what the rules do when the person above goes away.

applications.title: Notice slow harm
applications.text: Poison by degrees leaves no moment to point at. Look at what has been getting slightly worse for months and name it, since nothing will announce itself.

applications.title: Be careful with grief that is performed loudly
applications.text: Amalickiah pretended to be wroth and had the mourning turned into a manhunt inside a minute. When the person most visibly upset is also the one directing what happens next, that combination is worth a pause.

applications.title: Do not take flight as a confession
applications.text: The servants' escape was offered to the queen as evidence in itself: "does not this testify against them?" People run because they are frightened about as often as because they are guilty, so ask what they were running from before you read the running as an answer.

questions.text: What am I refusing to do out of fear, and which fear is larger?
What plan have I laid in my heart that I have not said out loud?
What have I agreed to on the fourth ask that I refused three times?
What rule in my situation would change everything if someone exploited it?
What kindness of mine could be used against me?
Where have I called something skill that was closer to fraud?
What have I been taught that I am currently living beneath?
